one_liner: C implementation of OMG DDS brokerless pub/sub over UDP; one 2023 vendor-adjacent test measured ~37x Kafka's small-message rate.
what_it_does: Cyclone DDS implements the OMG Data Distribution Service: typed publish/subscribe between DomainParticipants, DataWriters and DataReaders on named topics. Peers find each other through zero-configuration discovery (multicast when the network allows it) and talk over the interoperable DDSI-RTPS wire protocol, so it can interoperate with other DDS implementations. Types are defined in IDL and compiled with the bundled idlc generator (the Python binding can define them at runtime). Per-reader and per-writer QoS covers reliability, history, deadline, liveliness, ownership and DDS Security. The core is a C API; C++ (OMG ISO C++ API) and Python bindings live in sibling repos. It is not a Kafka replacement: there is no broker, no on-disk log, no offsets and no consumer groups, and the only durability is transient-local data held in the live writer's history cache.
how_it_is_fast: There is no broker hop and no log append. A writer sends DDSI-RTPS submessages straight to the readers over UDP, switching to IP multicast when several readers need the same data. By default the whole path from dds_write (CDR serialization, writer history cache insert, packing) to sendmsg runs on the calling thread. The xpack stage packs many DATA, DATAFRAG and HEARTBEAT submessages into one datagram of up to MaxMessageSize, using a scatter/gather list that references the serialized data rather than copying it. On receive, one recv thread reads into large receive buffers with a bump allocator that resets once nothing in the datagram is still live, so nothing is copied until the serdata is built. By default (SynchronousDeliveryLatencyBound=inf) data is delivered to reader caches from that thread instead of going through a delivery queue. Writer-history nodes and xmsg objects are cached because, per the design notes, the allocator became the bottleneck above 1M samples/s. An optional PSMX plugin (iceoryx or iceoryx2) adds zero-copy shared-memory loans for traffic on the same host.
when_to_use: Small-message pub/sub on one host or a LAN where a broker hop is too slow. In the 2023 test it ran 2.1-2.5M msg/s at 8-64 B on localhost, against Kafka's ~62K.
Latency-sensitive control loops: 8 us vs Kafka's 73 us one-way (64 B ping-pong, localhost), and 38 us vs 84 us over 100GbE.
ROS 2 robotics: rmw_cyclonedds_cpp is a fully supported RMW that ships in ROS 2 binary releases. Fast DDS, not Cyclone, is the default RMW.

Systems that need the DDS standard itself: DDSI-RTPS interop with other vendors, IDL/XTypes type checking and evolution, deadline/liveliness/ownership QoS, and DDS Security (authentication, access control, encryption).
Large payloads between processes on the same host, using the iceoryx/iceoryx2 shared-memory plugin, as long as the types are fixed-size.
when_not_to_use: You need Kafka's durable, replayable, partitioned log. Transient-local history dies with the writer, the docs say there is no native service for transient or persistent data, and DDS 'partitions' are naming scopes, not shards with offsets.
Traffic over routed networks, the Internet or WiFi. The same paper calls multicast discovery less suitable there because it floods, and WiFi falls back to multicast for discovery (SPDP) only.

Very large deployments without careful discovery tuning. One report (#2306, open) describes about 500 processes on 100 machines causing 50-100 MB/s discovery bursts and one process growing to 45 GB of RAM.

Multi-MB samples on stock kernel settings, especially best-effort. Losing one datagram drops the whole sample, and the ROS 2 docs and issues #2139/#1993 need a larger rmem_max and SocketReceiveBufferSize to fix it.

Maximum raw throughput. In the same study Zenoh peer mode had about 2x its bitrate, and Cyclone's single-machine bitrate fell from 25.8 Gbps at 256 KiB to about 9 Gbps at 32-64 MiB, well under the 76 Gbps iperf ceiling.

integration.form: shared lib (libddsc, built with CMake; static and FetchContent builds are supported) plus the idlc code generator
integration.dependencies: none at runtime for the core. Build needs CMake 3.16+. Optional: OpenSSL (DDS Security plugins, TLS/TCP), iceoryx 2.0 or iceoryx2 (shared-memory PSMX plugin, loaded dynamically since 11.0). The C++ and Python bindings are separate repos.
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler and CMake 3.16. MSVC older than VS 2019 builds without the restrict keyword, which disables some performance optimizations.
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows are in CI (Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 with gcc/clang, macOS 14, Windows 2022/2025 with VS 2022). The README also lists *BSD, QNX, OpenIndiana and Solaris 'with some caveats', and the source tree has FreeRTOS/lwIP, Zephyr and VxWorks ports. The iceoryx shared-memory path does not work on Windows.
integration.thread_safety: The docs I read give no blanket statement. dds.h says several threads may block on one waitset at once, and marks topic filter setters as not thread-safe against concurrent reads and writes. Calling dds_set_listener(entity, NULL) from that entity's own listener callback deadlocks (reproduced in #2374).

gotchas: The defaults are not tuned for throughput: MaxMessageSize is 14720 B, FragmentSize 1344 B, WhcHigh 500 kB and the socket receive buffer request 1 MiB. The README says the WhcHigh default is 'a bit small to get really high throughput', and the paper kept most options at their defaults.

Multicast is used for discovery and for data to several readers on wired interfaces, and many switches drop multicast more readily than unicast, per the maintainer in #1993. Use AllowMulticast to limit it (for example to spdp only) or turn it off.

Samples larger than MaxSampleSize are dropped with only a log warning, and the receiver still acknowledges them. Readers get only a 'sample lost' flag on the next sample, which the docs call easy to overlook.

The network-facing parsers have had security bugs: CVE-2024-10838 (OOB read in DDS Security deserialization, fixed per a March 2025 advisory) and XML-parser CVEs before 0.8.0. Open 2026 issues (#2427, #2432, #2445, #2453) report malformed XCDR payloads being accepted.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Over Zenoh, pick it when you need standard DDS (vendor interop over DDSI-RTPS, IDL types, DDS QoS) or a ROS 2 LAN setup, or when the lowest same-host latency matters (8 us vs Zenoh P2P's 10 us). Zenoh doubled its throughput, beat it across machines (16 vs 38 us) and handles routed networks better. Over Eclipse Mosquitto, it has no broker, lower latency (8 vs 27 us) and ~3x the bitrate at 32 KiB (23.1 vs 7.6 Gbps). Against Redpanda, Woodpecker or other Kafka-style logs it only makes sense when you do not need durability or replay.
verified_claims_summary: An arXiv v1 preprint (2303.09419, March 2023) by ZettaScale's Zenoh Taiwan team and NTU compared Cyclone DDS with Kafka 3.2.1. ZettaScale was then the main Cyclone DDS developer. Cyclone ran brokerless and mostly on defaults, with RELIABLE and KEEP_ALL for throughput and one take per loop; its version is not stated. Kafka was a single broker driven by rust-rdkafka 0.28.0 with acks=0, linger.ms=0 and no compression. Hardware was a Ryzen 7 5800X fixed at 4.0 GHz on Ubuntu 20.04, on localhost and on 3 machines over 100GbE. The appendix tables give 2.3M vs 61.6K msg/s at 8 B (~37x) and 23.1 vs 3.6 Gbps at 32 KiB (~6.4x) on one machine, 13.9 vs 4.6 Gbps at 32 KiB (~3x) across machines, and 64 B latency of 8 vs 73 us (one machine) and 38 vs 84 us (across machines). No compiler or flags are given, the benchmark code now returns 404, and Kafka could not run above 512 KiB. The paper's DDS programs were based on Cyclone's official examples, and Cyclone's own benchmarking docs say its throughput/latency examples 'sacrifice performance for simplicity' and should not be compared with results from other tools, so the DDS figures are not a clean measurement in either direction.
status_note: Actively maintained Eclipse project (11.0.1 released 2026-03-20, master commits through 2026-09-25) under EPL-2.0 OR BSD-3-Clause, but 80 of the last 100 commits come from one maintainer and 21 months passed between 0.10.5 and 11.0.0, which left ROS 2 Humble users asking for 0.10.x fixes (#2325).
